A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
religion is not a direct cause of counterterrorism cooperation, but that the institutional relationship between religion and the state is an indirect cause.

the United States is able to build counterterrorism cooperation with states where religion-state ties are weak and the state is able and willing to repress or ignore the religious sector, but not with states where religion is more politically relevant.

The main takeaway from our work is that
religion matters in international relations, but it matters in ways that are different from the ways in which we have previously thought about it.
we must pay attention to the institutional context in which religion is organized in order to understand the role of religion in international affairs.
